question: What makes a continuous query fundamentally different from a one-time DBMS query?
options: It can only execute SQL without WHERE
It is registered to process arriving stream data over time and may maintain evolving results or output streams
It always sees the complete future stream before producing output
It must permanently store every record
explanation: Continuous queries keep running as data arrives; one-time queries are evaluated over a fixed data snapshot.
source: L2 Stream Processing, slides 7–9, 35–38; Babcock et al., §2.1.

question: Which operator requires state even when each incoming event is processed individually?
options: A map that converts Celsius to Fahrenheit
A filter that forwards temperature > 30
A running count of events per weather station
A field projection of stationName
explanation: The count for a station depends on preceding events. A pure map, filter and projection can process records independently.
source: L2 Stream Processing, slides 13–19 and 60–69; Flink, chapter 2 (stateless/stateful operators).

question: For arrivals A1, B1, A2, B2, A3, which is the count-based sliding window of size 3 immediately after B2?
explanation: After four arrivals the most recent three are arrivals 2–4. [A1,B1,A2] is the prior window, not the one after B2.

question: What distinguishes a tumbling count window of 3 from a sliding count window of 3 with slide 1?
options: Tumbling windows can never aggregate data
A tumbling window groups non-overlapping triples; sliding windows overlap and reuse events in successive windows
Sliding windows use timestamps while tumbling windows cannot
Both produce identical membership and output timing
explanation: With records A,B,C,D, a tumbling window completes [A,B,C], whereas the rolling length-3 window next contains [B,C,D].
source: L2 Stream Processing, slides 20–26; Golab & Özsu, §3.1.

question: A mobile sensor records events at 10:01–10:03 while offline and sends them all at 10:10. Which claim is correct?
options: Event time necessarily equals the server arrival time
Event-time windows use event timestamps; processing-time windows use the operator clock, so assignments can differ
Both window types always reconstruct the same minutes
The events cannot be processed because they are late
explanation: Event time captures when something happened; processing time captures when the engine observes/processes it. Late data policy affects handling.
source: L2 Stream Processing, slides 28–35; Flink, chapter 2 (time semantics).

question: In event-time stream processing, what is the best interpretation of a watermark with timestamp T?
options: A cryptographic proof that no earlier-timestamp event can arrive
A progress estimate/assumption used to determine when event-time operations may advance
An instruction to permanently stop every query
The processing-time clock of the CPU
explanation: Watermarks signal expected event-time progress. Straggling events can still arrive later, so engines need late-event policies.
source: L2 Stream Processing, slides 29–36; Flink, chapter 2 (watermarks).

question: When might an approximate synopsis be preferable to an exact stream computation?
options: When the query can be answered exactly with zero state
When bounded memory or input rate prevents exact historical computation and the application can tolerate controlled error
Whenever the developer dislikes writing SQL
Only when queries are one-time and never run on streams
explanation: Sampling, histograms and sketches trade fidelity for resource use. Approximation should reflect the application’s acceptable error, not convenience.
source: L2 Stream Processing, slides 44–48; Babcock et al., §§4.1–4.3 and 6.

question: In the hospital stream-join example, why is dropping random events potentially dangerous under overload?
options: Dropping records always improves medical accuracy
All events have identical urgency and utility
Discarding urgent patients can undermine the critical results even if throughput improves
The join output is unaffected by filtering before the join
explanation: Load shedding needs application-aware QoS/utility choices; the lecture’s triage filter prioritizes critical patients rather than shedding indiscriminately.
source: L2 Stream Processing, slides 50–59 (hospital network, triage and QoS).

question: Why do distributed stateful Flink jobs need checkpoints when the live state is already kept in a state backend?
options: The backend automatically makes every side effect globally transactional
A checkpoint provides a recoverable, consistent state and source-position snapshot after failures
A checkpoint is identical to scaling out a worker
Checkpointing is needed only for stateless filters
explanation: Live local state can be lost when tasks fail. Distributed checkpoints and replayable inputs allow restoring a consistent logical computation.
source: L2 Stream Processing, slides 63–69 and 75–83; Flink, chapters 2–3.

question: Which statement about at-least-once versus exactly-once is accurate?
options: At-least-once means some records are processed zero times
Exactly-once managed state automatically guarantees an external email is sent once
At-least-once permits duplicates after replay; exactly-once managed state avoids duplicate logical effects in recovered state under its assumptions
Exactly-once means a system will never crash
explanation: Recovery may replay events; consistent snapshots prevent duplicate logical effects on managed state. External sinks require compatible guarantees.
source: L2 Stream Processing, slides 75–78; Flink, chapter 2 (consistency guarantees).
